items.new: In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles — among other ponderous things, a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift — this vast bunch of grapes was hoisted up to the main-top and firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended in stages over the side, Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

Almost invariably it is obliquely crossed and re-crossed all over with countless straight marks in thick array, something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. These are hieroglyphical; that is, if you call those mysterious ciphers on the walls of pyramids hieroglyphics, then that is the proper word to use here. I should say that those New England rocks on the sea-coast which Agassiz imagines to bear the marks of violent scraping contact with vast floating icebergs — I should say that those rocks must resemble the Sperm Whale not a little in this respect. items.new: A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces, called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is very apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better still, an Indian poncho slipped over his head and hanging down around his extremity. It is because of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is able to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of the North, if he were not supplied with his cozy overcoat? True, other fish are found to be exceedingly lively in those Hyperborean waters; but these, mind you, are your cold-blooded, lungless fish, whose very bellies are refrigerators; creatures that warm themselves in the lee of an iceberg, as a traveler in winter would bask before an inn fire; whereas, like man, the whale has lungs and warm blood. Freeze his blood, and he dies. How wonderful it is, then — except after explanation — that this great monster, to whom bodily warmth is as indispensable as it is to man; how wonderful that he should be found at home, immersed to his lips for life in those Arctic waters! — where, when seamen fall overboard, they are sometimes found months afterward, frozen upright into the hearts of fields of ice, as a fly is found glued in amber. But it is more surprising still to know, as has been proved by experiment, that the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.

items.new: He had originally been raised among the crazy society of Neskyeuna Shakers, where he had been a great prophet; in their cracked, secret meetings he had several times descended from heaven by way of a trap-door, announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket — but which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum. A strange, apostolic whim having seized him, he had left Neskyeuna for Nantucket, where, with that cunning peculiar to craziness, he put on a steady, common-sense exterior and offered himself as a green-hand candidate for the Jeroboam's whaling voyage. They took him on; but the moment the ship was out of sight of land, his insanity broke out in a flood. He announced himself as the archangel Gabriel, and ordered the captain to jump overboard. He published his manifesto, in which he proclaimed himself the deliverer of the isles of the sea and vicar-general of all Oceanica. The unflinching earnestness with which he declared these things — the dark, daring play of his sleepless, excited imagination, and all the preternatural terrors of real delirium — combined to invest this Gabriel, in the minds of most of the ignorant crew, with an atmosphere of sacredness. Moreover, they were afraid of him. As such a man, however, was not of much practical use in the ship, especially as he refused to work except when he pleased, the unbelieving captain would gladly have been rid of him; but on learning that the captain intended to land him at the first convenient port, the archangel at once opened all his seals and vials — devoting the ship and all hands to unconditional damnation if this intention was carried out. So strongly did he work upon his disciples among the crew that at last they went to the captain in a body and told him that if Gabriel was sent from the ship, not a man of them would remain. He was therefore forced to give up his plan. Nor would they allow Gabriel to be mistreated in any way, whatever he might say or do; so that it came about that Gabriel had the complete freedom of the ship. The consequence of all this was that the archangel cared little or nothing for the captain and mates; and since the epidemic had broken out, he was more high-handed than ever, declaring that the plague, as he called it, was at his sole command, and that it would not be stopped except at his good pleasure. The sailors, mostly poor devils, cringed, and some of them fawned before him; following his instructions, they sometimes paid him personal homage, as to a god. Such things may seem incredible; but, however astonishing, they are true. items.new: Nor was it long in coming. Tall spouts were seen to leeward, and two boats, Stubb's and Flask's, were sent off in pursuit. Pulling farther and farther away, they at last became almost invisible to the men at the masthead. But suddenly, in the distance, they saw a great heap of tumultuous white water, and soon after word came from aloft that one or both of the boats must be fast. An interval passed, and the boats were in plain sight, in the act of being dragged straight toward the ship by the towing whale. So close did the monster come to the hull that at first it seemed as if he meant it harm; but suddenly going down in a maelstrom within three rods of the planks, he wholly disappeared from view, as if diving under the keel. "Cut, cut!" was the cry from the ship to the boats, which for one instant seemed on the point of being dashed fatally against the vessel's side. But having plenty of line still in the tubs, and the whale not sounding very rapidly, they paid out plenty of rope, and at the same time pulled with all their might so as to get ahead of the ship. For a few minutes the struggle was intensely critical; for while they still slacked out the tightened line in one direction and still plied their oars in another, the opposing strain threatened to take them under. But it was only a few feet's advance they were trying to gain. And they stuck to it till they did gain it; when instantly a swift tremor was felt running like lightning along the keel, as the strained line, scraping beneath the ship, suddenly rose into view under her bows, snapping and quivering, and flinging off its drippings so that the drops fell like bits of broken glass on the water, while the whale beyond also rose into sight, and once more the boats were free to fly. But the exhausted whale slackened his speed, and, blindly changing his course, went around the stern of the ship, towing the two boats after him, so that they made a complete circuit.
